Salvador was founded by the Portuguese in 1549 and remained the capital of colonial Brazil for many years. Today, its historic centre offers a vivid glimpse of the city's past: Pelourinho, squares, churches, brightly painted facades and the changing elevation between Salvador's Upper and Lower Cities.

A walk through the city is closely connected with Afro-Brazilian culture. An itinerary can include music, capoeira, local cuisine and an introduction to Bahia's traditions before heading to the modern parts of the city and the coast.

Salvador works equally well as a cultural destination in its own right or as the starting point for a longer trip through Bahia. After several days in the city, the journey can continue with a beach holiday and other destinations in the state.

Samaipata lies about 120 km from Santa Cruz, in the foothills of the Andes. Green valleys and hills surround the town. Visitors come to discover local life and explore the El Fuerte archaeological complex.

El Fuerte de Samaipata is located near the town. The site was once a ceremonial and administrative centre. Carved images of animals, parallel grooves and water channels survive on its large rock surface. Steps and niches can also be seen here.

After exploring the complex, it is worth returning to Samaipata for lunch in town. A trip from Santa Cruz combines a walk among Andean hills, a visit to an ancient site and traditional Bolivian cuisine.

### Samaná Peninsula: pristine nature!

The Samaná Peninsula is a place of unspoiled natural beauty, with coconut groves, clear streams, waterfalls and caves. Its deserted beaches make it a destination for travelers who prefer independent, personalized holidays. Dolphins and manatees can be seen in the sea, and from January to March even humpback whales.

Beautiful beaches extend along almost the entire peninsula. Popular destinations include the southern coast and Cayo Levantado Island, as well as Playa Rincón, Playa Morón and Playa Bonita Beach on Samaná's northern coast.

## Holidays in Samaná

### Things to do in Samaná

In nearby Los Haitises National Park, visitors can swim in an underground lake while looking at ancient rock paintings on the cave walls. In the village of Las Terrenas, travelers can book several excursions, explore deserted beaches or head into the mountains. The area's main attraction, however, is the 30-metre El Limón waterfall.

At San Agustín de Callo Hacienda, it is tempting to linger beside the stone wall. Dark volcanic blocks fit tightly together: this is preserved Inca masonry. Colonial walls rise above, while greenery and flowers share the courtyard with old doors. Here, history can be discovered in the details that still form part of everyday life.

The hacienda is near Lasso, at the foot of Cotopaxi volcano, south of Quito. It was built on the site of an Inca palace and later served as an Augustinian monastery. The inner courtyard combines Inca architecture, Spanish colonial style and buildings from the republican era. The rooms with ancient stone walls are especially interesting to compare with the rest of the house.

Today, it is a working farm and a small hotel. A walk around the estate introduces rural Andean life, while views of Cotopaxi add to the experience of the building itself. The hacienda appeals to history enthusiasts and travelers seeking a peaceful stop between Ecuador's natural attractions. Lunch or an overnight stay should be arranged when planning the trip.
